title: Are Ryobi Power Tools Good? Ryobi Review: Yes, for Home Use
h1: Is Ryobi a Good Brand? Ryobi Tools Review
description: Yes, Ryobi is a good brand for homeowners: ONE+ batteries fit hundreds of tools and HP brushless models handle most DIY jobs, but pros need tougher tools.
dek: Yes, Ryobi is a good brand for homeowners: ONE+ batteries fit hundreds of tools and HP brushless models handle most DIY jobs, but pros need tougher tools.
intro: Yes, Ryobi is a good brand for homeowners and DIYers: its 18V ONE+ platform fits one battery to hundreds of tools, every ONE+ battery made since 1996 fits every ONE+ tool, and the HP brushless drills, impacts and trimmers have enough power for decks, fences and most remodeling. It is not built to take daily professional abuse the way Milwaukee or DeWalt tools are.

This review explains which Ryobi tools are worth buying, which to skip, how the batteries hold up, what owners complain about, and how Ryobi compares with the professional brands. Specs and warranty terms come from Ryobi's published information; durability notes reflect what owners commonly report.
quickAnswer: Ryobi power tools are good for homeowners, renters and hobbyists, and ONE+ is the best-value cordless platform for household use. Buy the HP brushless versions of drills, impacts and saws, and save on standard versions of lights, fans and inflators. Professionals who run tools all day should choose a pro platform instead.

sections.h: Is Ryobi a Good Brand? Ryobi Tools Review at a Glance

blocks.p: **Short answer:** yes, Ryobi is a good brand for homeowners, renters and hobbyists, and its 18V ONE+ system is the best-value cordless platform for household use. It is not the right main platform for professionals who run tools all day, because gearboxes, chucks, switches and housings are built to a price and wear sooner under jobsite abuse.

blocks.p: The honest verdict splits by tool. Ryobi's HP brushless drills, impact drivers, oscillating tools, trimmers, inflators, lights and household specialty tools are excellent for the money. Its standard brushed circular and reciprocating saws are where it feels most like a budget brand.

Anyone who uses power tools a few times a month: building a deck, assembling furniture, hanging shelves, trimming a quarter-acre lot, patching drywall. The breadth of the lineup means one set of batteries covers far more household jobs than any professional platform.

Contractors and tradespeople who need tools to survive daily drops, dust and long runtimes. Our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt comparison](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) explains what the extra money buys in those platforms.

sections.h: What Is Ryobi ONE+ and Why Does It Matter?

blocks.p: ONE+ is Ryobi's 18-volt battery platform, launched in 1996 with a simple pledge: any ONE+ battery fits any ONE+ tool, past or future. Ryobi has kept that promise through several battery chemistries and housing designs, which is rare in an industry that often changes battery shapes. A lithium pack bought today runs a ONE+ drill from many years ago, and older lithium packs run current tools. Early nickel-cadmium packs also fit, but deliver much less runtime and power.

It is the widest in the industry, with hundreds of tools. Beyond drills, saws and sanders, ONE+ includes glue guns, caulk guns, tire inflators, fans, work lights, speakers, hand vacuums, power scrubbers, soldering irons, a cordless nailer, a cooler and even a bug zapper. If a battery tool for the house exists, Ryobi probably makes one.

Ryobi power tools are made under license by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the group that also owns Milwaukee. The two brands are engineered and marketed separately, and their batteries do not interchange. Ryobi's role inside TTI is the consumer market, which is why it is priced and built for weekend users.

In the United States, mainly through Home Depot and Ryobi's own website, plus reconditioned tools through factory outlet channels. In Australia, Ryobi is sold mainly through Bunnings, and the same ONE+ compatibility rule applies there, which is why "Ryobi battery reviews Australia" and "Ryobi 18V drill reviews Australia" searches lead to the same platform discussed here. Single-retailer distribution keeps prices consistent and returns easy, but you will not find Ryobi at most independent hardware stores.

blocks.h3: Why compatibility is the real selling point

blocks.p: A platform that does not change shape protects your money. The batteries you buy for a drill will run a trimmer, a fan and an inflator years from now, and every bare tool you add costs less because you are not paying for another pack and charger.

sections.h: Are Ryobi Brushless (HP) Tools Worth It?

blocks.p: Yes, for any tool that works hard. Ryobi sells most core tools in two tiers. **Standard ONE+** tools are usually brushed, lighter on features and cheapest. **ONE+ HP** tools use brushless motors with more advanced electronics, and Ryobi designs them to draw more power from its high-performance batteries. Most HP tools are noticeably more compact and stronger than their standard versions.

A brushless motor turns more battery energy into work and less into heat, so it runs longer per charge and holds speed under load. The difference shows most when a drill spins a large spade bit, an impact driver sinks lag bolts, or a saw cuts thick or wet lumber. Owners commonly describe the HP drill and impact as a different class of tool from older brushed Ryobi models, and "Ryobi brushless tools review" searches usually end in that conclusion.

For light work, brushed tools do the job. A standard drill handles pilot holes, flat-pack furniture and shelf brackets. A standard oscillating tool or sander works for occasional trim and patch work. Lights, fans, glue guns and inflators gain nothing from brushless motors.

blocks.h3: Pair HP tools with the right pack

blocks.p: HP tools reach full performance on Ryobi's larger and high-output packs. An HP circular saw on a 1.5 or 2.0 amp-hour battery will run, but with less power under load and short runtime. Budget for at least one bigger pack if you buy high-draw HP tools.
Buy HP for drills, impact drivers, circular saws, reciprocating saws, grinders and string trimmers. Save money with standard versions of light-duty tools.

sections.h: Which Ryobi Tools Are Worth Buying?

blocks.p: The HP drill and impact driver, the household specialty tools, the oscillating multi-tool, the sander, the 18V yard tools and the AirStrike nailers are the strongest buys in the lineup.

blocks.h3: Ryobi 18V HP drill and impact driver

blocks.p: These are the heart of any kit. The HP versions are strong enough for decks, fences, small framing projects and long furniture builds, lighter and shorter than older Ryobi drills, and usually sold in kits with two batteries for far less than a professional kit. For most people searching "Ryobi 18V drill review," the answer is to buy the HP brushless kit rather than the basic brushed drill.

This is where Ryobi has no real rival. The inflator handles car tires, bike tires and balls. The glue gun, caulk gun and power scrubber speed up chores most people do by hand. Fans, work lights and the speaker are inexpensive add-ons that make the batteries useful every week, not just on project days.

Both are light-duty tools by nature, and Ryobi's versions handle flush cuts on door casings, trim notches, furniture sanding and patch smoothing well. Professional versions vibrate less and change blades faster, but occasional users rarely notice. Search interest in "Ryobi multi tool review" is high for good reason: it is one of the platform's best values.

The 18V HP string trimmer, hedge trimmer and blower suit small and medium lots. Many owners retire a gas trimmer on a quarter-acre lot this way. Our [weed eater guide](/best-weed-eater/) compares battery trimmers across brands if you are not committed yet.

They drive brad and finish nails without a compressor or gas cartridge. They fire slower than pneumatic nailers, but for trim, baseboard and small projects owners often call them one of the platform's best surprises.

Ryobi's ONE+ vacs are handy for cars and quick cleanups if you already own packs. For a garage or workshop, a corded unit with a wide hose usually does more; see our [shop vac guide](/best-shop-vac/).

sections.h: Which Ryobi Tools Should You Skip or Upgrade?

blocks.p: Skip the brushed versions of high-load saws, and use specialist brands where precision matters.

They cut plywood and two-by lumber, but they bog down in thick or wet stock and drain batteries quickly. A weak motor in a circular saw is not just slow; it binds more, which raises the risk of kickback. Buy the HP brushless saw or a corded saw if you cut regularly.

The basic brushed recip saw is fine for pruning and light demolition, but it vibrates more and struggles with nail-embedded lumber. Step up to the HP model, or a professional brand if demolition is a regular job.

Ryobi's table and miter saws work for rough carpentry, but finish carpenters often find fences, detents and blade alignment less precise than higher-end saws. For fine woodworking, a dedicated machine pays off, and the same applies to a planer; our [benchtop planer guide](/best-benchtop-planer/) covers the corded options.

Ryobi sells laser levels and stud finders, but specialist brands usually do these better. For mounting a TV or tiling a room, a well-rated tool from our [laser level](/best-laser-level/) and [stud finder](/best-stud-finder/) guides is a safer bet than whatever happens to run on your battery.

Ryobi's power tools are the draw. For sockets and wrenches, a dedicated hand-tool brand gives better quality per dollar, and for wheels and brakes you want a calibrated wrench from our [torque wrench guide](/best-torque-wrench/), not an impact driver.

Good for the money, as long as you match pack size to the tool and store them sensibly. ONE+ lithium packs come in compact 1.5 and 2.0 amp-hour sizes, larger 4.0 and 6.0 amp-hour sizes and beyond, plus HP high-performance packs built for brushless tools. Compact packs keep a drill light; large packs are for saws, trimmers and blowers. Most owners settle on two compact packs and one or two large ones.

blocks.h3: How long do Ryobi batteries last?

blocks.p: Lithium-ion packs wear with charge cycles, heat and age. A ONE+ pack in regular household use typically gives several years before capacity drops noticeably. Owners who report early failures often stored packs in hot cars or freezing sheds, or left them fully drained for months. Keep packs indoors, at partial charge, away from heat.

More than people think. Basic chargers can take several hours on a large pack. Ryobi's rapid and multi-port chargers cut that time substantially and are worth buying once you own big batteries. If a charger delays charging a hot pack right after heavy use, that is thermal protection doing its job.

No. Cheap ONE+ compatible packs sold online often lack the protection circuits and quality cells of genuine packs, which means weak performance and a real fire risk. They can also complicate a warranty claim if they damage a tool.

Ryobi regularly bundles packs with a free bare tool, especially around spring, Father's Day and the holidays. Buying batteries this way is often cheaper than buying the pack alone. Owners in Australia report similar promotions at Bunnings.

sections.h: Is Ryobi's 40V Outdoor Line Any Good?

blocks.p: Yes, for larger yards. Ryobi runs a separate 40V platform for mowers, chainsaws, blowers, string trimmers and snow blowers, plus an 80V platform for riding mowers. The 40V packs do not fit ONE+ tools, so this is a second battery system, built for homeowners who need more power and runtime than 18V tools deliver.

blocks.h3: How do the 40V mowers and blowers perform?

blocks.p: The 40V HP brushless mowers and blowers have become serious alternatives to gas on suburban lots. They start instantly, run quietly and need almost no maintenance. Runtime depends on pack size and grass conditions, and owners of larger lawns commonly add a second battery. For leaf cleanup, our [leaf vacuum guide](/best-leaf-vacuum/) compares battery and gas options.
Ryobi's 40V tools often carry a longer tool warranty than ONE+, frequently five years, with separate terms for batteries. Check the current terms for the exact model.
EGO's 56V platform is the main rival and is often stronger in mowers and blowers. Ryobi tends to cost less and is easier to bundle with promotions.

blocks.h3: Should a small yard bother with 40V?

blocks.p: No. On a quarter-acre lot, ONE+ HP trimmers, blowers and hedge trimmers do the job without a second set of batteries and chargers. Move to 40V only when you want a battery mower or heavier outdoor tools.

sections.h: What Do Ryobi Reviews and Complaints Say?

blocks.p: Most Ryobi reviews praise value, compatibility and the breadth of household tools. The recurring complaints are about durability under heavy use, the warranty process after the first few months and the performance of older brushed tools.

Owners consistently mention that the batteries fit everything, that the HP drill and impact are far better than expected, and that the specialty tools such as inflators, glue guns and scrubbers get used constantly. Many say they started with one kit and grew to a dozen tools without buying another charger.

ul: **Wear under heavy use.** Chucks, switches and gearboxes on lower-tier tools can wear sooner when pushed daily.
**Brushed saws.** Slow cuts and short runtime on thick stock come up again and again.
**Warranty process.** Many owners find a defective tool within the first 90 days is easiest to swap at Home Depot; after that, claims go through service centers and can take longer.
**Counterfeit batteries.** Off-brand packs bought online account for a share of battery complaints.

blocks.p: Most ONE+ tools carry a three-year limited warranty, and ONE+ batteries generally carry three years as well, with terms varying by product. Reconditioned tools from outlet channels usually have shorter coverage. Register tools and keep receipts.

blocks.h3: How long do Ryobi tools last?

blocks.p: With household use, owners commonly report drills and impacts lasting many years. Under daily professional use, life drops sharply. Storing tools indoors and keeping packs out of extreme heat helps more than any other habit.

sections.h: Ryobi vs Milwaukee, DeWalt and Ridgid: How Does It Compare?

blocks.p: Ryobi is cheaper and broader for household use; Milwaukee and DeWalt are tougher and better supported for daily work; Ridgid sits in between.

The professional brands build tools that survive jobsite drops and all-day runtime, carry longer or better-supported warranties and offer more trade specialty tools. Ryobi tools are usually less durable under daily use, sometimes a little heavier for the same output, and simpler in features, but they cost a fraction as much, and the gap grows with every tool you add. For a drill used a few times a month for a decade, that trade-off favors Ryobi. For a trade where downtime costs money, it favors the pros.

Ridgid power tools are also made by TTI and sold at Home Depot. They sit above Ryobi in price and build, and registered Ridgid tools can qualify for a lifetime service agreement. Ryobi has the bigger lineup and lower prices. Serious hobbyists who want more durability should compare both.
Both are closer to Ryobi in price, but neither matches the breadth of ONE+ or its long record of battery compatibility.

blocks.h3: The mixed kit most households end up with

blocks.p: Ryobi for the everyday power tools, a quality hand-tool set for mechanical work, and specialist tools where precision matters. That combination gets you most of a professional's capability for a fraction of the cost.

mistakes: Buying brushed saws for regular cutting

Standard brushed circular and reciprocating saws handle occasional cuts but slow down in thick or wet lumber and drain packs fast. A struggling saw also binds more, which raises kickback risk. If you will cut regularly, the HP brushless version costs a little more and performs far better.
Running high-draw tools on compact packs

A 1.5 or 2.0 amp-hour pack keeps a drill light, but on a circular saw, blower or trimmer it limits both power and runtime. Ryobi designs its HP tools to perform best on larger or high-output packs, so buy at least one big battery before you buy demanding tools.
Starting the 40V platform without needing it

Ryobi's 40V outdoor line uses different batteries from ONE+. On a small yard, ONE+ HP trimmers and blowers do the job, and you avoid paying for a second set of packs and chargers. Move to 40V only when you want a battery mower or heavier outdoor equipment.

Ryobi runs promotions often, especially in spring, around Father's Day and during holiday sales, with free bare tools bundled into battery kits and discounted combo kits. Buying outside those windows usually means paying noticeably more for the same tools and batteries. Plan purchases around the sale calendar.

Cheap ONE+ compatible packs sold online often lack protection circuits and quality cells, which means weak runtime and a real fire risk. They can also complicate warranty claims if a tool is damaged. Buy genuine Ryobi batteries, ideally during a battery-plus-free-tool promotion.
bottomLine: Ryobi is a good brand for anyone who uses power tools at home rather than on a jobsite. ONE+ gives you the widest lineup of battery tools on one pack, a compatibility promise that has held since 1996, frequent promotions and HP brushless tools strong enough for decks, fences and remodels. Buy HP for the tools that work hard, skip the brushed saws, add at least one large battery, and use specialist brands for measuring and hand tools. If you work in the trades, a professional platform will serve you better; for everyone else, Ryobi delivers more tool per dollar than anything else on the shelf.

faqs.a: Yes, for homeowners, renters and hobbyists. Ryobi's ONE+ platform offers the widest range of battery tools at the lowest prices, and every ONE+ battery fits every ONE+ tool. The HP brushless tools handle most DIY projects well. It is not the best choice for professionals who use tools all day, where Milwaukee, DeWalt or Ridgid hold up better.

faqs.q: Are Ryobi power tools good enough for remodeling?
faqs.a: For a homeowner doing their own remodel, yes, especially the HP brushless drills, impact drivers and saws. They handle framing small walls, hanging cabinets, building decks and similar work. Contractors who run tools daily will get longer life and better service from professional brands. Many DIY remodelers start with Ryobi and add specialist tools as needed.

faqs.q: Will a new Ryobi battery fit my old ONE+ tools?
faqs.a: Yes. Ryobi designed ONE+ so any ONE+ battery fits any ONE+ tool and has kept that compatibility since 1996. Current lithium packs run older tools, and older lithium packs run new tools. Early nickel-cadmium packs also fit but deliver far less runtime and power than current lithium batteries.

faqs.q: Is Ryobi HP worth the extra money?
faqs.a: For drills, impact drivers, circular saws, reciprocating saws and string trimmers, usually yes. The brushless motors deliver more power, run longer per charge and are more compact. For light-duty tools such as lights, fans, glue guns and inflators, the standard versions work just as well, so spend where the tool works hard.

faqs.q: How long do Ryobi tools last?
faqs.a: With household use, many owners report Ryobi drills and impact drivers lasting many years, and batteries typically give several years before capacity drops noticeably. Durability falls under daily professional use, where chucks, switches and gearboxes wear faster. Storing tools and packs indoors and away from heat extends their life considerably.

faqs.q: Are Ryobi batteries good in Australia?
faqs.a: Yes. Ryobi sells the same 18V ONE+ system in Australia, mainly through Bunnings, and the same rule applies: any ONE+ battery fits any ONE+ tool. Owners there report the same strengths and weaknesses as elsewhere, so buy genuine packs, match larger packs to high-draw tools and keep batteries out of hot cars and sheds.

faqs.q: What should my first Ryobi purchase be?
faqs.a: An 18V ONE+ HP brushless drill and impact driver kit with two batteries and a charger is the best start for most people. It covers drilling and driving for nearly every household job. Add a circular saw, an oscillating multi-tool and an inflator next, buying them as bare tools during promotions so you do not pay for extra chargers.
